What is Firebase and when would you use it?

Firebase is a Backend-as-a-Service on Google Cloud providing auth, real-time NoSQL databases, file storage, hosting, serverless functions, push messaging and app quality tools via client SDKs. It suits MVPs, mobile/web apps needing real-time sync or offline support, chat and collaboration features, and small teams wanting less backend infrastructure. For complex relational data, heavy reporting or strict backend control, a traditional API with a SQL database may be better – or a hybrid.
Firestore vs Realtime Database?

Realtime Database is a single JSON tree with very low-latency sync, simple queries (one sort/filter key) and bandwidth-based pricing. Firestore uses documents and collections, supports richer compound queries, aggregations, transactions, offline support, automatic scaling and multi-region replication, billed per operation. Firestore is the default for new projects; RTDB still fits presence systems or many tiny, frequent updates.
How does Firebase Authentication work end to end?

The client signs in with a provider through the Firebase SDK and receives an ID token (JWT, one-hour expiry) plus a refresh token that the SDK uses to renew it. Firebase services read the token automatically and expose it as request.auth in security rules. Your own backend receives the token in the Authorization header and verifies it with the Admin SDK, getting the uid and custom claims.
How do you verify a Firebase ID token in a Spring Boot backend?

Initialise FirebaseApp with Application Default Credentials, then in a Spring Security filter extract the Bearer token and call FirebaseAuth.getInstance().verifyIdToken(token) (pass true to also check revocation). On success build an Authentication from the uid and custom claims; on FirebaseAuthException return 401. Alternatively use spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server with the issuer https://securetoken.google.com/<projectId>, since the tokens are standard JWTs.
What are custom claims and how do you implement roles?

Custom claims are extra key/values (max 1000 bytes) embedded in a user's ID token, set only from a trusted environment with the Admin SDK: setCustomUserClaims(uid, Map.of("role","admin")). They appear in request.auth.token in rules and in the verified token on your backend. The client must refresh its token (getIdToken(true)) to see new claims.
What are security rules and why are they critical?

Since web and mobile clients access Firestore, RTDB and Storage directly, rules are the only server-side gate on who can read or write which data and in what shape. They check authentication, ownership, roles via claims, and validate incoming fields. Misconfigured rules (e.g. open test-mode rules) are a common cause of data leaks; test them with the emulator and unit tests before deploying.
"Rules are not filters" – what does that mean?

Firestore doesn't silently drop documents a user can't read; it evaluates whether the query could return any forbidden document and rejects the whole query if so. Therefore if rules require resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid, the client query must include where('ownerId', '==', uid), otherwise it fails with permission-denied.
How do real-time listeners work and what should you watch out for?

onSnapshot (or AngularFire's collectionData) opens a listener that delivers the initial result and then every change, including local pending writes for latency compensation. Each document returned and each change counts as a read. Always unsubscribe when the component is destroyed, limit and paginate listened queries, and avoid listening to large collections.
How do you model data in Firestore?

Model for your queries: documents in top-level collections or subcollections (e.g. rooms/{id}/messages), denormalise frequently displayed fields since there are no joins, and keep documents small (1 MiB limit). Use subcollections or separate collections for unbounded lists rather than huge arrays. Use transactions or batched writes to keep duplicated data consistent, or Cloud Functions triggers to fan out updates.
Transactions vs batched writes in Firestore?

A transaction reads documents and then writes based on those values; it retries automatically if data changed concurrently (e.g. decrement stock only if available). A batched write groups multiple writes (set/update/delete) that succeed or fail atomically without reads. Both are atomic; batched writes can be queued while offline, but transactions require a connection.
What are Cloud Functions used for in a Firebase app?

Trusted server-side logic that shouldn't run in the client: sending emails or FCM messages, processing payments with secret keys, maintaining counters and denormalised data on Firestore triggers, resizing uploaded images on Storage triggers, setting custom claims on user creation, and scheduled cleanup. Handlers must be idempotent because event delivery is at least once.
How do push notifications with FCM work?

The app requests notification permission and gets an FCM registration token, which it sends to the backend to store per user/device. The backend sends messages via the FCM HTTP v1 API or Admin SDK to a token, topic or condition; FCM routes them through APNs on iOS and the service worker on web. Notification payloads display automatically in the background, data payloads are handled by app code; clean up tokens that return unregistered errors.
How do you use Firebase in an Ionic app?

The Firebase JS SDK / AngularFire works inside the Capacitor WebView for Firestore and most Auth flows. For native-only capabilities – Google/Apple native sign-in, push notifications, Crashlytics, Analytics – use Capacitor plugins (e.g. @capacitor-firebase/authentication, @capacitor-firebase/messaging) and add google-services.json and GoogleService-Info.plist to the Android and iOS projects. Popup/redirect web sign-in is unreliable in WebViews, which is why native plugins are preferred.
Is it a problem that the Firebase apiKey is visible in the front-end code?

No – the Firebase config including apiKey only identifies the project; it does not grant access to data. Protection comes from security rules, Firebase Auth, App Check and API key restrictions in the Google Cloud console. Service account keys and Admin SDK credentials, by contrast, are real secrets and must never be in client code.
What are common Firebase pricing pitfalls?

Firestore charges per document read, so unbounded listeners, reading whole collections to count, and N+1 read patterns in the UI inflate costs; use limit, pagination, aggregation queries and caching. Cloud Functions in loops (a trigger writing to the collection that triggers it) can run away. Use Blaze plan budget alerts and monitor usage dashboards, remembering that budgets alert but do not stop billing.
What are Firestore's main limits?

Documents max 1 MiB; about one sustained write per second to the same document (use distributed counters for hot counters); queries need indexes and some combinations need composite indexes; no native full-text search or server-side joins; and the database location is fixed at creation. Large analytics are better exported to BigQuery.
When would you combine Firebase with your own Spring Boot backend?

When you want Firebase's auth, real-time sync or FCM but also need complex business logic, relational data in MySQL/PostgreSQL, third-party integrations with secrets, or reporting. The front end authenticates with Firebase and calls the Spring Boot API with the ID token; the backend verifies it, applies authorisation, and uses the Admin SDK to write to Firestore or send FCM messages where needed.
💡 Keep one source of truth per piece of data to avoid sync problems between Firestore and SQL.
How do you sign a user out of all devices, or block a disabled user immediately?

ID tokens are self-contained JWTs valid for about one hour, so disabling a user does not invalidate tokens already issued. Call admin.auth().revokeRefreshTokens(uid) (or FirebaseAuth.revokeRefreshTokens in Java), which stops refreshes and records a revocation time. To reject already-issued ID tokens before they expire, verify with verifyIdToken(token, true) on your backend, and in security rules compare request.auth.token.auth_time with a revocation timestamp you store per user. Checking revocation costs an extra lookup, so do it on sensitive endpoints.
ID token or session cookie for a server-rendered app?

The client SDK keeps the ID token in the browser and refreshes it automatically, which suits SPAs calling APIs with a Bearer header. For server-side rendering (Angular SSR, a traditional web app), exchange the fresh ID token once for a session cookie with createSessionCookie(idToken, {expiresIn}), valid from 5 minutes to 2 weeks, set it as HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite, and verify it on each request with verifySessionCookie(cookie, true). Because it is a cookie, add CSRF protection.
What is anonymous authentication, and how do you keep the user's data when they sign up later?

Anonymous auth gives a visitor a real uid without credentials, so security rules and per-user data (a cart, a draft) work immediately. When they register, call linkWithCredential (or linkWithPopup) on the current user: the anonymous account is upgraded and keeps the same uid, so no data migration is needed. If the credential already belongs to another account, linking fails with credential-already-in-use and you must merge data yourself. Clean up abandoned anonymous accounts periodically; Identity Platform can delete them automatically.
Why can sequential document ids or timestamp fields limit Firestore write throughput?

Firestore splits data by key ranges. Monotonically increasing document ids, or an indexed field like createdAt written at a high rate, send every write to the same end of the range, creating a hotspot. Use the auto-generated random ids, and for very high write rates on a collection with an increasing indexed field, exempt that field from indexing or spread writes (for example a shard prefix). Ramp up traffic gradually (the "500/50/5" guideline: start at 500 writes per second and grow by 50% every 5 minutes) so Firestore can split ranges. Separately, a single document sustains only about one write per second; use distributed counters for hot documents.
How do you evolve the data model in Firestore without a schema migration tool?

Old and new document shapes coexist, so code must handle both. Common approach: add a schemaVersion field; make readers tolerate missing fields with defaults; write new fields from the new version of the app; then backfill existing documents with a one-off Admin SDK script using BulkWriter (batched, rate-limited, retrying). Remove old fields only after every client version still in use (mobile apps update slowly) no longer reads them, and tighten security rules last. For heavier changes, a Cloud Function can migrate documents lazily on write.
Why does a collection group query fail with permission-denied even though the user can read each document?

Rules written as match /posts/{postId}/comments/{commentId} apply to that path only. A collection group query is evaluated against a recursive wildcard, so you need a rule such as match /{path=**}/comments/{commentId} { allow read: if resource.data.visibility == 'public'; }. Remember that rules are not filters: the query's own where clauses must guarantee every possible result passes the rule. A collection-group index is also required.
How do you back up Firestore and recover from a bad deployment that corrupted data?

Enable point-in-time recovery (PITR), which keeps versions for up to 7 days so you can read data as of an earlier time and write it back, and schedule managed exports (or scheduled backups) to Cloud Storage for long-term retention; exports can be imported into another project or loaded into BigQuery. Exports are not atomic snapshots across a busy database, so use PITR for precise restores. Test the restore process, and protect against the main cause of corruption with rules tests, staged rollouts and validation in Cloud Functions.
How do you protect a Cloud Function from abuse?

For onCall functions, check request.auth (and custom claims) at the start and throw HttpsError('unauthenticated') or 'permission-denied'; enable enforceAppCheck: true so only your genuine app can call it. For onRequest HTTP functions, verify the ID token yourself, restrict CORS, and keep public endpoints idempotent. Validate inputs, set maxInstances to cap cost from traffic spikes, and add budget alerts, because a loop or attack on a pay-per-use function shows up on the bill.
Client SDK vs Admin SDK: what is the real difference?

| Client SDK (web, Android, iOS) | Admin SDK (Java, Node.js, Python, Go)
Runs in | The user's browser or phone | A trusted server: Spring Boot, Cloud Functions
Acts as | The signed-in user | A service account
Security rules | Checked on every read and write | Bypassed completely
Can do | What the rules allow for that user | Create users, set custom claims, verify ID tokens, send FCM, read anything
Secret material | None (the apiKey only identifies the project) | Service account credentials, which must never leave the server
FirebaseToken t = FirebaseAuth.getInstance().verifyIdToken(idToken, true); // true = check revocation
FirebaseAuth.getInstance().setCustomUserClaims(t.getUid(), Map.of("role", "doctor"));
Rule of thumb: rules protect client access only. Anything the Admin SDK does must be authorised by your own code, for example with Spring Security roles taken from custom claims.
Callable (onCall) vs HTTPS (onRequest) vs event-triggered Cloud Functions?

| onCall | onRequest | Event trigger (Firestore, Auth, Storage, Pub/Sub)
Called by | The Firebase client SDK (httpsCallable) | Any HTTP client: webhooks, curl, other servers | The platform, when the event happens
Auth | ID token verified for you; auth context provided | You verify the Authorization header yourself | No caller; runs with admin privileges
App Check | Can be enforced with an option | Manual | Not applicable
Delivery | Once per call; the client handles retries | Once per call; the caller handles retries | At least once: the handler must be idempotent
Typical use | A business action from your app (place order) | Payment webhooks, a small public API | Send mail on a new document, keep counters, clean up files
Rule of thumb: onCall for your own app, onRequest for callers outside Firebase, triggers for reactions to data changes. Never let a trigger write the same document that fires it without a guard, or it loops.
Firebase Auth vs Security Rules vs App Check: what does each protect?

| Firebase Auth | Security Rules | App Check
Question it answers | Who is the user? | May this user do this to this document? | Is this request coming from my real app?
Mechanism | ID token (signed JWT) | Rules evaluated by Firebase on each request | Device or browser attestation (Play Integrity, App Attest, reCAPTCHA Enterprise) gives an App Check token
Stops | Anonymous access to user-only data | Users reading or changing other users' data | Scripts that reuse your public config outside the app
Does not stop | A signed-in user abusing access | Abuse within what the rules allow | A real user on a real device; it is not authentication
Your own backend | Verify the ID token | Not applied: code the checks yourself | Must verify the App Check token itself
Rule of thumb: use all three in layers. Auth identifies, rules authorise, App Check reduces bot and quota abuse.
Firebase vs Supabase vs your own Spring Boot + MySQL backend?

| Firebase | Supabase | Spring Boot + MySQL
Database | Firestore: document NoSQL | PostgreSQL: relational | MySQL, fully under your control
Access control | Security Rules | Postgres Row Level Security policies | Spring Security in your code
Queries | No joins, limited query shapes | Full SQL | Full SQL, JPA
Real-time | Built-in listeners | Built-in (database changes over WebSocket) | You build it (WebSocket, SSE)
Lock-in | Google only | Open source, can be self-hosted | None
Best fit | Mobile and real-time apps, small teams | Relational data with BaaS speed | Complex domain, strict audit and compliance, many integrations
Interview tip: a BaaS saves you writing auth and CRUD, but every business rule must fit its rule language. For an EHR-style domain with heavy validation and reporting, a custom backend is usually easier to reason about.
